title: Why Your Antenatal Visits Are Non-Negotiable
author: Caremed Connect Team
excerpt: Skipping a check-up might seem harmless, but regular antenatal care is the single most important thing you can do for a safe pregnancy and delivery.
content: Pregnancy is a journey of constant change, and routine antenatal visits are your roadmap to a safe delivery. These appointments aren't just about checking your weight or blood pressure—they are vital for catching potential complications like pre-eclampsia or gestational diabetes early.

During these visits, your healthcare provider monitors the growth of your baby, checks your general health, and offers essential advice on nutrition, exercise, and birth planning. It also gives you the chance to ask questions and ease any anxieties you may have about labor.

In Nigeria, we recommend at least four focused visits for a healthy pregnancy, but more might be needed if you have underlying health conditions. Caremed Connect partners with Amuwo Odofin Maternal & Child Centre to ensure you have access to skilled professionals who can guide you every step of the way.
Remember, a healthy mother equals a healthy baby. Don't wait for an emergency to see a doctor—prevention is always better than cure.

title: Foods to Eat and Avoid in Your First Trimester
author: Caremed Connect Team
excerpt: Navigating pregnancy cravings can be tricky. Here’s a simple guide to what should be on your plate—and what you should steer clear of—in those crucial first three months.
content: The first trimester is a period of rapid development for your baby, and your diet plays a huge role. Focus on eating plenty of folate-rich foods like leafy greens and legumes, as folic acid helps prevent neural tube defects.

Incorporate proteins like lean meat, fish, and beans to support tissue growth. However, you must avoid raw or undercooked meats and eggs due to the risk of bacteria. Also, limit your intake of high-mercury fish like shark or mackerel.

While it's tempting to reach for that cup of coffee, try to reduce your caffeine intake to less than 200mg per day. And most importantly, avoid alcohol entirely—there is no known safe amount during pregnancy.

Proper nutrition reduces the risk of birth defects and keeps your energy levels up. If you're unsure about your diet, our nutritionists at Caremed Connect are just a WhatsApp message away to help you plan safe, delicious meals.

title: 6 Warning Signs During Pregnancy You Should Never Ignore
author: Caremed Connect Team
excerpt: While some discomforts are normal, certain symptoms are red flags. If you experience any of these, contact your doctor immediately.
content: Pregnancy comes with aches and pains, but how do you know when it's serious? There are specific warning signs that require immediate medical attention, not just a call to your friend or a search on Google.

Look out for severe headaches that don't go away, blurred vision, or sudden swelling in your face and hands, which could indicate pre-eclampsia. Also, be alert for vaginal bleeding, severe stomach pain, or painful contractions happening before 37 weeks.

If your baby’s movements have significantly slowed down or stopped entirely, do not wait for morning. Similarly, a fever over 100.4°F (38°C) or a feeling of dizziness/fainting should be treated as an emergency.

title: Postnatal Care: What Happens Right After Birth
author: Caremed Connect Team
excerpt: The journey doesn't end at delivery. Postnatal care is critical for monitoring the health of both you and your newborn in those first few hours and weeks.
content: The first 24 hours after delivery are a rollercoaster of emotions. But medically, this is a critical time for monitoring. Your medical team will check your blood pressure, pulse, and temperature frequently to ensure you aren't experiencing postpartum hemorrhage or infection.

For your baby, doctors will administer essential newborn care, including Vitamin K injections, eye ointment to prevent infections, and the first vaccines (BCG and OPV). A hearing test and a full physical examination are also usually performed.
Breastfeeding is often established within this time. Don't hesitate to ask your midwife for help with latching. It is a learning process for both you and your baby.

We ensure every mother at Amuwo Odofin Maternal & Child Centre receives comprehensive postnatal support. Remember to book your follow-up appointment for 6 weeks postpartum—it's essential for checking your recovery and your baby's growth.

title: Understanding Gestational Diabetes Screening
author: Caremed Connect Team
excerpt: Gestational diabetes affects millions of pregnancies, but it is manageable. Here’s what the Glucose Tolerance Test involves and why it’s so important.
content: Gestational diabetes is a type of high blood sugar that develops during pregnancy and usually goes away after birth. However, it can cause serious complications—like a large baby, premature delivery, or pre-eclampsia—if left undetected.

Screening typically occurs between 24 and 28 weeks of pregnancy. The Oral Glucose Tolerance Test (OGTT) involves fasting overnight, drinking a sugary solution, and having your blood drawn two hours later to see how your body handles sugar.
If you are diagnosed, don't panic. Most women manage this condition with a healthy diet, regular exercise, and frequent blood sugar monitoring. In some cases, insulin may be prescribed.

title: Childhood Vaccination Schedule in Nigeria: A Parent's Checklist
author: Caremed Connect Team
excerpt: Vaccines save lives. Here is the recommended immunization schedule from birth to 12 months to protect your child from preventable diseases.
content: Vaccination is one of the most effective ways to protect your child from deadly diseases. In Nigeria, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA) recommends a strict schedule to ensure immunity is built at the right time.

At birth, your baby needs the BCG (against tuberculosis) and Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) 0. At 6 weeks, the vaccination schedule includes Penta (Diphtheria, Pertussis, Tetanus, Hepatitis B, HIB), Pneumococcal, and Rotavirus vaccines.
The process continues with boosters at 10 weeks, 14 weeks, and 9 months (Measles and Yellow Fever). It is crucial to keep the vaccination card safe and to show it at every clinic visit.
Caremed Connect is committed to vaccination. We offer these life-saving vaccines at our partner clinics. Don't postpone or skip appointments—vaccinate your child to secure their future.

title: Managing Morning Sickness: Tips for Relief
author: Caremed Connect Team
excerpt: Nausea and vomiting are common in early pregnancy, but you don't have to suffer in silence. Try these simple tips to get through the day.
content: Despite the name, morning sickness can strike at any time of the day. It is caused by hormonal changes, particularly the rise in hCG and estrogen, and usually peaks in the first trimester.
To manage it, try eating small, frequent meals rather than three large ones. Keep dry crackers by your bedside and eat one before you even get up in the morning to settle your stomach.
Ginger is a natural and effective remedy. Try ginger tea or ginger sweets. Avoid strong smells that trigger nausea, and stay well hydrated by sipping water or clear fluids throughout the day.

If you are vomiting so much that you can't keep anything down, you may have hyperemesis gravidarum, which requires medical attention. Caremed Connect can connect you with a doctor if your symptoms become severe.

title: What to Pack in Your Hospital Bag: Your Third-Trimester Checklist
author: Caremed Connect Team
excerpt: Your due date is approaching, and the adrenaline is kicking in. Packing your hospital bag early saves you stress and ensures you have everything you need.
content: Aim to have your hospital bag packed by the time you reach 36 weeks. You never know when labor might start, and being prepared will give you peace of mind.
For mom, pack comfortable nightgowns, a robe, slippers, maternity pads, nursing bras, and a going-home outfit. Don't forget your toiletries and a phone charger with a long cable.
For baby, you’ll need onesies, socks, a swaddle blanket, a going-home outfit, diapers, and wipes. Also, bring essential documents like your ID, health insurance card, and your antenatal care records.

Caremed Connect recommends bringing snacks and a water bottle for dad or your birthing partner. Having a prepared bag means you can focus on what matters most—a smooth delivery at Amuwo Odofin Maternal & Child Centre.

title: The Importance of Iron and Folic Acid During Pregnancy
author: Caremed Connect Team
excerpt: Your body needs extra nutrients to support your baby's growth. Here is why iron and folic acid are the two essential supplements you can't do without.
content: Iron is vital for making hemoglobin, the protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen to your tissues and your baby. During pregnancy, your blood volume increases significantly, so iron is crucial to prevent anemia, which can cause fatigue and increase the risk of premature birth.
Folic acid (Vitamin B9) is essential in the early weeks for the development of the baby’s brain and spinal cord. It significantly reduces the risk of neural tube defects.
The recommended daily dose is usually 400-800 mcg of folic acid and 27 mg of iron. However, your doctor might adjust this based on your specific blood tests.

Ensure you are taking your supplements daily, ideally with vitamin C (like orange juice) to help with iron absorption. Caremed Connect provides high-quality prenatal vitamins to keep you and your baby strong.

title: Water Birth: What Are the Benefits and Risks?
author: Caremed Connect Team
excerpt: Water birth is becoming a popular option for pain relief. We weigh the pros and cons to help you decide if it's the right choice for you.
content: Water birth involves laboring and delivering your baby in a warm tub of water. Many women love it for the natural pain relief it provides—the warm water relaxes muscles, reduces stress, and often allows mothers to move more freely during contractions.
Proponents believe it lowers blood pressure, reduces the need for epidurals, and gives the mother a sense of control. The baby tends to emerge into a warm, gentle environment that mimics the womb.

However, it's not for everyone. You need to be considered low-risk to have a water birth. Risks include the difficulty of monitoring the baby's heart rate continuously and the rare chance of infection or water embolism.
If you are interested in a water birth, discuss it with your healthcare provider at Caremed Connect. We can assess your eligibility and guide you on the best birth plan for your situation.
